opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I have pretty mixed feelings about it. I understand why it happens. When a big company releases something impressive, there's huge pressure, especially on students, to show that you can reproduce it or get close to it. That kind of work has some value: it helps the community understand what actually matters in these systems, and open reproductions can be really important for science.

But if your whole research agenda becomes "catch up with the big labs," I think you've already lost something. Academia will almost never win on compute, data, or engineering headcount. If you play that game, you're always a step or two behind, and by the time you catch up, the frontier has moved again. It's exhausting, and it doesn't make the best use of what academic researchers are good at.

What I tell my students is to ask a different question: what are the problems that big companies *aren't* incentivized to work on, or are too committed to their current path to rethink? Things like new representations, new learning paradigms, better evaluation, understanding why things work, or areas like visual intelligence and world modeling where the recipe isn't settled. A lot of the most influential ideas came from small groups who were willing to look somewhere else, not from people trying to match a leaderboard number.

So I'd say: catching up can be a means, a way to learn the tools and build intuition. But it shouldn't be the end goal. The goal should be to find your own question, something you genuinely believe matters, and have the patience to pursue it even when it's not what everyone else is doing.

r001.rationale: The response says catch-up pressure leads researchers to reproduce or get close to company releases, then explains that academia will almost never match their resources and will remain behind. Together, these statements convey that catch-up efforts may amount to reproduction when matching the companies is out of reach.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's the wrong framing, and I try very hard not to let my own group fall into that mode. If your whole research agenda is defined by what OpenAI or Google did last quarter, you've already lost, because they have a hundred times the compute and the people, and by the time you reproduce their result they've moved on. You end up doing the work after the fact, and you learn very little about what actually matters.

What I think academia and smaller labs are actually good at is asking questions that big companies have no incentive to ask. The companies are optimizing for a product and for a scaling curve. They don't have the time, or frankly the freedom, to go back and ask, "wait, why does this component work at all? Do we even need it?" Those are the questions I find interesting. When we did ConvNeXt, the point wasn't to beat the transformer, it was to ask whether the gain really came from attention or from everything else that changed around it. A lot of that was about understanding, not winning a benchmark.

And the other thing is that the landscape shifts. Everyone was doing contrastive learning, and then two years later representation learning looks like a solved problem to people, and then suddenly it comes back because the generative models need better representations. If you're only chasing, you're never positioned for those turns. If you've been working on the fundamental question, you're already there when the field comes around.

So I'd say: don't catch up, differentiate. Pick the problems where being small is an advantage, where you can be careful, you can be a little stubborn, and you can afford to be wrong for a while. That's where the real contributions come from. The reproductions and the open-source efforts matter too, I don't want to dismiss them, but they shouldn't be the identity of a research group.

r001.rationale: The response says smaller labs lack the compute and people to keep pace, and that by the time they reproduce a large company’s result, the company has moved on—so catch-up research becomes after-the-fact reproduction.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s important to ask what we’re actually trying to catch up with. If the goal is simply to reproduce what a large company has already done, then you’re letting their resources and priorities define your research agenda. You might learn a lot in the process, but you’ll always be chasing a moving target.

For an academic lab, I think the more interesting question is: what can we investigate that isn’t getting attention there? Can we challenge an assumption, understand why something works, or test an idea that looks too uncertain to prioritize in a product roadmap? You still need to understand what industry is doing. But that should inform your questions, rather than determine them.

So I wouldn’t dismiss catching up entirely. Sometimes reproducing a result gives you the foundation to discover something new. I just don’t think catching up should be the destination.

r001.rationale: The response says that trying to catch up may mean reproducing what a company has already done, but does not connect that reproduction to catching up proving unattainable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish catching up as a way to learn from catching up as a research goal. Reproducing a strong system can teach you a lot. But if your whole agenda is defined by what a large company has already done, you’re always chasing a moving target—and usually with fewer resources.

For me, the more interesting question is: what can we investigate that they’re not investigating? Can we challenge an assumption, understand why something works, or explore an idea that doesn’t yet make sense at their scale? You don’t necessarily need to compete on the same axis.

Of course, that’s difficult. A benchmark gives you a very clear target; an original question is much less certain. But I think that uncertainty is part of research. Catching up can be a starting point. I wouldn’t want it to become the destination.

r001.rationale: The response says reproducing a strong system can be useful and that catching up is a moving target, but it does not say research becomes reproduction when catching up proves unattainable.
